transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-21
Start: 14:30 PT
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen, Ravi Patel (Redwood); Aisha Rahman, Tom Keller, Mei Wu, Jorge Martinez, Priya Singh (Nebula Labs)

Summary:
Nebula reported intermittent CUDA timeouts and apparent KV cache 'collapse' under load when running quantized Llama-variant models in their on-prem VPC. Redwood SE walked through likely root causes (stream starvation, eviction noise from batching, quantization memory patterns), proposed a triage plan (repro harness, driver captures, controlled batch/seq-length matrix) and discussed retry semantics and graceful fallback policies.

Topics:
- Observed failures: soft OOMs, GPU watchdog resets, Cuda timeout errors (appear during peak batch windows)
- KV cache behaviour: evictions concurrent with large prefix reuse, appearing as "KV cash shrink" in logs
- Batching + prioritization: how continuous batching causes stream starvation in mixed-tenant pools
- Quantization: int8 memory layout causing transient memory spikes with large past sequences
- Retry semantics: idempotency, backoff windows, canary config for fallback to smaller model/quantized variant
- On-prem/VPC constraints: limited spare capacity, strict kernel versions, KMS accessibility concerns

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): okay, hi everyone thanks for joining, um I'll hand off to Ravi for the deep dive.
[00:12] Ravi (Redwood SE): hey all, hi Nebula team. quick note — I'll apologize in advance, my wifi is a little flakey. so what's the canonical symptom? Aisha?
[00:22] Aisha (Nebula): yeah so we've been seeing intermittent segfault-ish watchdog resets, sometimes labelled as C-U-D-A timeout in the container logs, sometimes the instance just drops. tends to happen around heavy batching windows when many short-chat sessions hit the same model.
[00:39] Tom (Nebula SRE): to add — we see dmesg lines with 'GPU hung' followed by a device reset. not always correlating with peak gpu util; it's more like when seq len and prefix reuse combine.
[00:53] Ravi: good, that matches a class of issues we've seen where KV cache thrash plus kernel launch latency produces starvation on the stream. basically one stream gets blocked while prefetches/evictions run on another and watchdog thinks it's hung.
[01:12] Mei (Nebula): we've been using an int8 quantized runtime on our private cluster — could quantization cause a memory spike?
[01:20] Ravi: yes, int8 layouts can still have transient temporary allocations — especially around attention recompute and rotary caches — if your runtime does not pre-allocate the KV scratch the allocator may fragment. that fragmentation + a big prefix can look like a soft-oom.
[01:36] Jorge (DevOps): our infra is fairly tight on capacity, we can't just add spare GPUs. what's the immediate mitigation?
[01:44] Ravi: short term — reduce batch ceiling and enforce per-request token caps, enable prefix-aware caching so the same prefix shares KV entries instead of duplicating. also tune stream priority so control/cleanup tasks get higher scheduler weight.
[02:02] Tom: can you explain stream priority? we run a multi-tenant pool in VPC with NVIDIA MIG and some dedicated instances.
[02:10] Ravi: sure — CUDA streams have scheduling hierarchies; if long-running kernels saturate a high-priority stream you can starve lower-priority housekeeping streams. we recommend isolating KV maintenance on a dedicated stream and bumping its priority so eviction/pre-fetch tasks can preempt heavy generation kernels briefly. it's a bit subtle and depends on your driver and runtime version.
[02:30] Priya (Security): any security concerns for changing stream behaviors?
[02:35] Maya: not directly. but for private deployments we always check that any changes don't require new kernel modules or relaxed driver privileges. if it does, we route that through the Private deployment team and schedule a maintenance window.
[02:47] Aisha: we also notice that when we have a sudden burst, some sessions see very long tail latency before the reset, not immediate OOM. is that consistent?
[02:55] Ravi: yup that's the 'watchdog sees a kernel launch wait' pattern; it accumulates until the kernel misses the watchdog threshold. there's often a latent period where the RK (runtime kernel) is queuing.
[03:12] Tom: in our logs we sometimes see 'KV cache shrink 0x1f' followed by 'alloc failed' — is that a real log name?
[03:20] Ravi: heh yeah 'KV cash' is actually commonly mis-typed in a bunch of older agents, but the point is your runtime is trying to evict entries and then failing to re-alloc. we need the full allocator trace.
[03:34] Mei: what's the right capture? we can gather container logs but what's most helpful?
[03:40] Ravi: nvprof/cuda-memcheck traces, the dmesg and kernel ring buffer, and the model runtime's trace that includes sequence lengths and batch size at time of failure. also the driver version and CUDA version. we sent a checklist earlier — we'll re-share a small script to collect the right flags.
[03:57] Maya: action item — I'll reshare the debug-capture checklist and a small repro template.
[04:04] Aisha: cool. about retry, can the platform retry safely? we care about idempotency for these chat sessions.
[04:11] Maya: good call — idempotency matters. our recommended retry semantics for generation requests are: conservative immediate backoff (exponential) with token-window preservation; if a request times out we attempt one immediate retry with smaller batch parameters, then escalate to fallback model variant if second attempt fails.
[04:29] Tom: would fallback be to a smaller model or quantized? we already run int8 in prod.
[04:36] Ravi: fallback options are configurable — smaller model (less memory) or a variant with disabled KV caching and smaller max prefix. it's a trade-off: accuracy vs stability. we often suggest canarying fallback on 1% of traffic first.
[04:51] Priya: any encryption/KMS repercussions when transferring logs off-prem for debugging?
[04:56] Maya: we recommend redacting PII and using signed temporary S3 links with your KMS in place; we can also accept a bundle uploaded to your private S3 with cross-account role. we'll provide a minimal set.
[05:08] Jorge: driver versions — we're on R520 and Ubuntu 20.04 kernel 5.15. is that a red flag?
[05:15] Ravi: R520 is okay but there are fixes in R525+ for stream preemption and watchdog latency thresholds; there's also some backports in the kernel that help the scheduler. upgrading isn't required but it's on the troubleshooting checklist.
[05:28] Aisha: curious — could CPU side GC pauses cause this? we saw long GC pauses in Python runtimes during heavy batching.
[05:36] Ravi: yes, GC or host-blocking I/O that blocks the host thread responsible for launching kernels will delay launches, worsening perceived hangs. ensure the host thread that enqueues kernels is pinned and uses minimal blocking operations.
[05:49] Mei: our setup uses a local KV cache and a background prefetcher. do you think prefetcher could be contributing?
[05:56] Ravi: absolutely — if prefetcher aggressively evicts and re-populates KV entries while generation kernels run, you'll get interleaved GPU mem ops that increase fragmentation. Consider throttling prefetcher concurrency and making it preemptible.
[06:10] Tom: any recommendations about watchdog thresholds? can we increase it safely?
[06:15] Ravi: you can increase the watchdog timeout but it's a band-aid; it hides underlying stream starvation. however for on-prem with tight SLAs it's an acceptable mitigation while you triage. document any increase and tie it to a canary.
[06:28] Aisha: ok let's talk about the repro plan.
[06:31] Ravi: step 1: reproduce on a controlled staging pool with identical driver/kernel. step 2: run a matrix of (batch size, prefix length, concurrent sessions) and capture nvprof + dmesg. step 3: toggle KV cache on/off and quantization mode. step 4: if repro replicates, try stream priority isolation and smaller batch ceilings.
[06:53] Jorge: timing — how much time to get the harness?
[06:56] Ravi: we'll send the template today, should take your team a couple hours to plug in.
[07:02] Maya: note — when you run the harness, please use the exact model binary checksum so we can match behavior.
[07:09] Tom: question about retries — if a request is partially filled (some tokens generated) and then the worker resets, what's the recommended behavior for the client?
[07:18] Maya: recommended: mark request with idempotency token, persist successful chunks as they stream, on retry attempt continue from last known token with smaller chunk size; if you can't resume reliably fallback to returning an explicit error to the end-user to avoid duplication.
[07:34] Aisha: about logs we saw two consecutive device resets in a short window, then service flapped for 10 minutes — is that typical of fragmentation?
[07:42] Ravi: repeated resets usually indicate the allocator kept failing to reclaim memory or there was a low-level driver issue; fragmentation causing cascading OOMs is possible especially with mixed tensor layouts.
[07:55] Mei: are there known model shapes that are worse? long prefix + multi-turn with cached past is the pattern right?
[08:02] Ravi: yep. also decoder-only models with large rotary caches and long attention windows are more susceptible.
[08:10] Tom: can we temporally disable kv cache for certain tenants?
[08:14] Ravi: yes you can expose it as a per-route flag in your router; Redwood clients often do route-level overrides to disable KV caching for specific customers or sequences.
[08:24] Jorge: that helps. what about quantization toggles — can we mix int8 and int4 models in same pool?
[08:31] Ravi: mixing quantization levels in same process can be messy due to different kernel code paths and allocator patterns; safe approach is separate pool or dedicated process per quantization flavor.
[08:42] Priya: security question: does collecting nvprof traces create any risk of secrets leaking?
[08:47] Maya: typically nvprof shows performance counters and memory addresses — not app-level secrets. still, follow your internal redaction rules.
[08:56] Aisha: let's run through a quick triage checklist you suggested — what do we need to capture?
[09:00] Ravi: checklist: exact model binary + checksum, driver CUDA version, kernel version, full dmesg and journalctl output, container logs, nvprof or Nsight output, runtime trace with per-request seq len and batch size, and host-level metrics during failure (cpu, mem, iowait).
[09:23] Tom: will attach.
[09:25] Maya: one gotcha — if you see 'cudaErrorLaunchTimeout' often the stack traces in the runtime could be truncated; ask for the runtime's internal event loop trace as well.
[09:35] Ravi: also include a sample of successful request traces to compare the scheduler behavior.
[09:41] Aisha: switching gears — we sometimes see 'context eviction' logs after a device reset, leading to longer recovery. thoughts?
[09:48] Ravi: context eviction after reset is expensive because it forces recreating contexts, reloading weights; reducing frequency of resets helps but you can also configure faster context restoration via warmed checkpoints and smaller model shards.
[10:03] Mei: any low-risk config flags we could flip without redeploy?
[10:07] Ravi: you can lower the batch_max and disable background prefetcher in runtime config at runtime. also enable stricter per-request token caps.
[10:15] Tom: question — is there a recommended backoff policy lambda for retries? say X attempts with Y base?
[10:22] Maya: common pattern: immediate retry with 200-500ms jittered exponential backoff, second retry with 2s base, then circuit-breaker escalation. keep retry attempts low to avoid amplifying load.
[10:34] Aisha: about monitoring — what signals tell us this is happening before reset?
[10:39] Ravi: rising async queue lengths, sustained kernel launch latencies, sudden drop in effective GPU occupancy while memory usage spikes; also repeated small GC/alloc failures in logs. those are early warning signs.
[10:55] Jorge: can Redwood's console surface these traces?
[10:58] Maya: we can ingest kernel-level traces via an upload and surface token/latency breakdowns; for hosted customers we push more structured telemetry. for Private we provide guides to ship to your observability stack.
[11:12] Mei: if we need a temporary workaround can Redwood route traffic to a hosted variant while we debug?
[11:18] Maya: yes for certain enterprise customers we can offer a hosted canary for a subset of traffic, but that depends on data residency and contracts. we'll check contract limitations.
[11:27] Priya: confirm — we can't send raw customer PII to hosted without an agreement.
[11:31] Maya: correct.
[11:33] Tom: what about kernel patches — could backporting a scheduler change be required?
[11:38] Ravi: sometimes yes, especially on older kernels; but try runtime-level mitigations first. kernel patches are a last-resort and require maintenance windows.
[11:46] Aisha: ok, let's prioritize running the harness. any tips for running it under load without risking prod?
[11:54] Ravi: run in dedicated staging cluster with same driver/kernel, use synthetic traffic generator matching your seq-length distribution. avoid hitting prod GPUs. also keep a guardrail to auto-pause the harness if resets exceed a threshold.
[12:10] Jorge: do you have a recommended harness?
[12:13] Ravi: yes, we'll attach a python harness that replays request traces with adjustable concurrency, batch ceiling, and prefix length. it includes optional nvprof hooks.
[12:24] Mei: do we need to change any RBAC to collect kernel logs?
[12:28] Maya: you might need sudo to gather dmesg; for container logs ensure your logging agent has access. we'll list required permissions.
[12:36] Aisha: if we identify it's driver-level, what's the rollback plan?
[12:40] Ravi: rollback plan: revert to snapshot with previous driver, if that's not possible we do pool-level isolation and route traffic to dedicated instances with known-good drivers.
[12:52] Tom: ok. another quick question — we saw 'cuda memcopy' stalls listed frequently, is that a sign of NVLink saturation?
[12:58] Ravi: could be NVLink or PCIe contention. look at host-side PCIe errors and NVLink counters. if using multi-GPU model shards, interconnects matter.
[13:10] Priya: timeline for follow up?
[13:12] Maya: we propose a 30-min repro session on 2026-10-29 to walk through your first harness run.
[13:18] Aisha: that works.
[13:21] Ravi: perfect. now I'll call out some subtle logs you might have missed...
[13:25] (Ravi walks through example log snippets — some lines mis-typed in transcript)
[15:40] Ravi: example snippet: "alloc failed: tried 0x7ff... size 0x1a00000, eviction attempt idx 3" — if you see repeated attempts it's fragmentation.
[16:05] Tom: we have a follow-up about workload shaping — can Redwood recommend rate-limiting knobs?
[16:11] Maya: yes — per-route QPS caps, smoothening token emission, and enforced per-connection concurrency. you can also implement an admission controller that rejects over-sized requests with 429.
[16:26] Aisha: final question — any advice on observability additions that catch fragmentation before resets?
[16:31] Ravi: add a metric for contiguous free memory blocks (via allocator metrics), track kernel launch latency percentile, and instrument KV cache hit/miss ratio per-prefix. those give early signals.
[16:48] Mei: got it.
[16:50] Maya: let's recap next steps quickly.
[16:53] Maya: 1) Redwood share repro harness & debug checklist (Maya/Ravi) 2) Nebula run harness and collect traces (Aisha/Jorge) 3) Redwood and Nebula do repro session 2026-10-29 4) If repro, try stream-priority isolation and small batch ceilings 5) Escalate to driver upgrade if needed.
[17:20] Aisha: thanks all. any last minute notes?
[17:23] Priya: will coordinate with legal on data transfer boundaries.
[17:26] Maya: thanks everyone.
[17:28] (meeting ends)
